https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: John Kampfner is a British author, broadcaster and commentator. His new book, “Braver New World: The Countries Daring to Do Things Others Won’t,” was published in April. He is a regular POLITICO columnist. Picking up a recent issue of German weekly Der Spiegel, the cover seemed to scream. “Germany’s Most Dangerous Man,” it shouted, the bold words emblazoned below a photo of the far-right Alternative for Germany party’s (AfD) Ulrich Siegmund. The intention was clear: A warning for both Germans and the world regarding the consequences of a far-right victory in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, as Siegmund seems poised to become his party’s first regional leader after the upcoming election there. Advertisement Advertisement The strategy clearly backfired. Siegmund’s allies bought up as many copies of the magazine as they could, so he could sign them in front of adoring crowds. But the underlying sentiment was not wrong — what happens in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 will affect all of Germany, Europe and the wider world. Polling at 42 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, that the AfD will emerge as the strongest force in this regional election is now beyond doubt — that’s around double the support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU). The Left party, another insurgent group, comes in third in the polling, while Merz’s coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), barely sit above the 5-percent threshold originally intended to keep out extremists, and the Greens are hovering perilously around that limit. Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), campaigns prior to state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on August 19, 2026 in Dessau-Rosslau. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images The arithmetic is convoluted but crucial. If the SPD and the Greens make the cut, the various mainstream parties could cobble together enough seats to run the state. But if they don’t, the AfD will be able to govern either on its own or possibly with the support of the far-left social conservative grouping Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht, which is also hovering right below the 5-percent threshold. The latter outcome would precipitate a political crisis across Germany not seen in decades. But it doesn’t end there. Two weeks after Saxony-Anhalt, voters will head to the polls in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and in the once reliably leftist city-region of Berlin, which is showing strong AfD support as well. This means that in the coming weeks or months, Germany could be faced with a collapsing government and even an ousted or replaced Merz — a move with little precedent in recent German history. And stuck with its stuttering economy, the country that prizes stability above all else is preparing to panic. Advertisement Advertisement Two world leaders are watching all this with anticipation: Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump. Relations between Germany and Russia have sharply deteriorated since 2022’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the latest discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport has sharply increased the hostility. But despite the consensus at the top of government that the Kremlin is carrying out a wider campaign of hybrid warfare across Europe — and four decades spent under Moscow’s yoke — many voters in the former German Democratic Republic retain strong affection for the country. The AfD is pushing that agenda hard. Although foreign policy falls under the federal government’s jurisdiction, Siegmund has been calling for an end to sanctions against Russia. He also intends to bring back Russian language classes in schools and wants Russian students to return to Germany as part of exchange programs. As for Ukrainians, he wants them designated as illegal migrants rather than refugees from war. A resident checks his phone in a container facility for refugees and asylum seekers located in aircraft hangars of the former Tempelhof airport in Berlin on August 14, 2025. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images Meanwhile, Trump, who has denounced Western Europe as socially reprobate, has made no secret of backing what his National Security Strategy calls “patriotic forces.” Quick to support European parties mirroring his own MAGA movement, his administration has been cultivating relationships and contacts with the AfD. Both these leaders have a vested interest in the party’s success. They view the AfD — and Europe’s other ultra-conservative groupings — as a bridgehead. And Siegmund fits into that perfectly. One of his party’s rising stars, the 35-year-old former salesman has a carefully curated image — riding East German-made Simson motorbikes to appeal to the young, while promising elderly voters to bring their “good, old, secure Germany back” — and the highest number of TikTok followers of any German politician. Advertisement Advertisement His party’s 150-page program for governing Saxony-Anhalt does not lack in ambition either. In it, Siegmund calls for Trump-style mass deportations of asylum-seekers — even though Saxony-Anhalt is one of the most ethnically homogeneous parts of the country, with only 1-in-13 citizens of migratory background. He promises to defund public broadcasters deemed hostile and unpatriotic, ban all symbols of “woke” culture — including pride flags — in schools and, as part of his fight against “the extinction of the German people,” offer tax breaks for families consisting of “a father, a mother and as many children as possible.” In an echo of the 1930s, the program even slams the Bauhaus art movement, which has strong roots in the region, as part of broader plans to promote “German art.” These are all agenda items Germany’s federal states have jurisdiction over within their specific regions — education, culture, certain aspects of policing and criminal justice. But to solely focus on these formal powers would be to miss the point. As in so many other countries, the far-right’s allure in Germany is growing, poisoning and often paralyzing the country’s mainstream parties and politics. Postwar Germany faced — and surmounted — a series of difficult challenges during the Cold War and the collapse of the Berlin Wall. Its constitution is rigorous, and its commitment to democratic values (not least its unstinting support for Ukraine) is impressive. But it would not be an exaggeration to say, as I sign off my last monthly column for POLITICO, that the country is about to enter one of its most dangerous moments yet. Trending WARREN -- In his welcoming remarks at the third annual Catholic Charities Regional Agency's Chefs for Charity fundraiser Sept. 17 at the St. Demetrios Community Center, Youngstown Bishop David J Bonnar encompassed the hall's atmosphere when he said, "One of the most sacred places in every home is the dining room table. It is the place where we gather as a family to share a meal and be sustained not just through the food prepared but the conversation that takes place that feeds the human heart. "As bishop, I want to welcome you to our table this evening where we gather to share a meal and do even more, especially for our community. There is a saying, 'Everything tastes better when it is eaten together.'" Bonnar ate with his family. Three of his siblings and extended family traveled from Pittsburgh to attend the charitable endeavor. The event included 22 food stations offering samples from Mahoning Valley restaurants and catering services. Culinary selections included Beef Barbacoa Tacos from The Lake Club in Poland; Wolf Wings with a sauce bar from The Blue Wolf Tavern in Boardman; Lollipop Lamb Chops from Station Square Ristorante in Liberty; Roasted Pumpkin Rigatoni A La Vodka from Casa Di Canzonetta in downtown Youngstown; Pork Souvlaki over Rice Pilaf from Jeffrey Chrystal Catering in Youngstown; and Butter Cake from Aqua Pazzo in Boardman. Julian Davis and Dina Kimbrough of Boardman said this was the first time that they came to this fundraiser. "We will be back," Davis said. He said sampling the food made him want to visit the restaurants that were represented. Kimbrough said, "I always like to give back when I can. This was a nice wholesome event." Bonnar agreed about the food offerings. "We know that taste is often influenced by the skills of those who prepare it. Tonight, we are blessed to have the best of the best with us from restaurants here in the Valley. I assure you that the many selections of food provided here this evening from their hands will taste delicious and bring joy to the heart. "The fruits of their labors, the generous sharing of their gifts along with the food they are providing tonight goes far beyond this extended table. For you see, the proceeds from this endeavor will assist the poor and needy in our community with housing assistance." Michele Puccetti of Niles and her daughter, Kristen Pucetti of Pittsburgh, and their friend, Carla Cicero of Niles, attended all three Chefs for Charity events. The rest of their table included additional family members. Cicero said that not only is she happy to help the charity but, "the food is wonderful." Besides the variety of delectable food, a basket gift raffle and a cash raffle took place while John Reese and Backbeat provided the music. Nick Frankos of Buena Vista Cafe in Warren expressed the overall feeling of the chefs in attendance at the community center. "These are all my brothers here," he said, then pointed out the main reason behind the event. "This is for Catholic Charities to help the community." His daughter, Selena Frankos, added, "This is an important cause for us to be a part of because it helps people in need." The food offered an opportunity not only to nourish the people who attended, but the money raised will help numerous people in Columbiana, Mahoning and Trumbull Counties combat homelessness.
